title: Table Headers and Relationships
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of table headers and relationships in a browser document.
Apply at least one relevant rule from this lesson to a small HTML example.
Check the result using browser inspection, a validator, or an accessibility checklist.

content.intro: This lesson turns “Table Headers and Relationships” into a practical authoring skill. You will work with column headers, understand the choices that matter, and check the result instead of relying on guesswork.
content.why_it_matters: Tables and forms carry structured data. Semantic relationships and understandable constraints improve both usability and the reliability of information sent to an application.

content_blocks.title: Accessible data table
content_blocks.alt_text: Use th for headers, td for values, and scope or explicit relationships when needed.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: The headers attribute: associates a data cell with one or more header-cell IDs in complex tables.

items.title: The scope attribute
items.text: The scope attribute: declares whether a table header applies to its row, column, row group, or column group.

items.title: Associating complex headers using id and headers
items.text: The headers attribute: associates a data cell with one or more header-cell IDs in complex tables.

items.title: Improving table navigation for assistive technology
items.text: Improving table navigation for assistive technology is one of the decisions covered by Table Headers and Relationships. Decide what the markup is meant to communicate, choose the native HTML structure that expresses that meaning, and verify the result in a browser or a relevant validation checklist. Avoid using an element or attribute just because its default appearance seems convenient.

items.title: Writing useful table captions
items.text: Include the media controls people need and alternatives to important audio or visual information. Check format support, file paths, caption timing, and permission/privacy needs.

content_blocks.title: Keep in mind
content_blocks.text: Prefer the native semantic element that communicates intent. Do not choose markup solely for its default visual style.

content.task: Create a small HTML example that demonstrates table headers and relationships. Keep the markup minimal, give every element a clear purpose, and inspect the rendered result.
task_acceptance_criteria: Use the relevant concept from Table Headers and Relationships.
Keep IDs unique and use valid nesting.
Check the result in a browser and record one finding.

troubleshooting.symptom: The expected content does not appear.
troubleshooting.check: Confirm the file was saved with an .html extension and inspect its path and nesting.
Check the resolved URL and confirm the referenced file or external resource exists and allows the request.

troubleshooting.symptom: The page looks correct but the markup may be invalid.
troubleshooting.check: Run the Nu Html Checker and follow its first relevant diagnostic, then validate again.

common_mistakes.why: The default appearance is not the element’s main meaning and can make navigation or maintenance harder.
common_mistakes.fix: Choose the element that matches the content purpose, then use CSS for presentation.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming a browser’s recovery means the source is valid
common_mistakes.why: Browsers often recover from malformed markup, which can hide defects and produce unexpected document structure.
common_mistakes.fix: Inspect the rendered DOM and run a validator against the original source.

common_mistakes.why: Missing files, narrow viewports, keyboard access, invalid input, or other states can expose defects.
common_mistakes.fix: Check the expected state plus one realistic edge case and an accessibility path.

summary: Table Headers and Relationships is about expressing document structure or behavior intentionally.
Include the media controls people need and alternatives to important audio or visual information. Check format support, file paths, caption timing, and permission/privacy needs.
Verify both markup and behavior; do not infer correctness from appearance alone.
